en: A certain Yakṣa, whose greatness had been eclipsed by his lord’s curse— to be endured for a year— as punishment for his negligence in his official duties,
took up residence in the hermitages of Rāmagiri, where the waters were sanctified by the bathing of Janaka’s daughter and the trees provided cool shade.
On that mountain, having spent several months separated from his beloved, that lover— his forearms marked by the scars where golden bracelets had slipped off—
beheld on the first day of the month of Āṣāḍha a cloud embracing the peaks, as beautiful to behold as an elephant turned back during the sport of trumpeting in a mud-bank.
Standing somehow before him for the sake of supporting the *ketaka* flower, the attendant of the King of Kings brooded for a long time with tears welling within;
for at the sight of a cloud, the mind of even a happy man undergoes a change—how much more so when the person longing for an embrace around one's neck is situated far away?
When the rainy season was near, he who sought to sustain the life of his beloved by means of a cloud, wishing to send news consisting of his own welfare,
joyfully addressed words of welcome preceded by affection to that cloud, for whom he had prepared an offering of fresh *kuṭaja* flowers.
"Where is a cloud—a mere conjunction of smoke, light, water, and wind—and where are the meanings of a message, which must be delivered by living beings with functional senses?
Thus, disregarding such considerations out of eagerness, the Guhyaka made his request; for those afflicted by desire are naturally wretched toward both sentient and insentient things.
Born in the world-renowned lineage of the Puṣkarāvartaka clouds, I know you to be the natural companion of Indra, able to assume any form at will.

Therefore, though my kinsmen are far away, I have come to you as a suppliant by the power of fate; for a request made to one of superior merit is better than a fulfilled desire obtained from a base person.
O cloud, you are the refuge for those who are tormented; therefore, carry my message to my beloved, who has been separated from me by the wrath of the Lord of Wealth.
You must go to her dwelling named Alakā, where the palaces are washed by the moonlight from the head of Hara as he stays in the outer gardens.
When you have ascended to the path of the wind, the wives of travelers, drawing back their long tresses and breathing a sigh of relief through trust, will gaze upon you;
for who, when you are thus prepared, would neglect his wife distressed by separation—unless he were another person like me, whose livelihood is dependent on others?
The favorable breeze gently stirs you as it blows, and this sweet-voiced *cātaka* bird, sharing your fragrance, warbles melodiously;
surely the cranes, forming a line in the sky through their long acquaintance with the moment of conception, will attend upon you who are so pleasing to the eye.
And you, whose progress is unhindered, will surely see your brother’s wife—faithful to her one husband, intent on counting the days, and unharmed.
For the bond of hope generally restrains the flower-like heart of women, which is prone to yielding immediately in separation from its beloved.
And having heard your thunder, so pleasing to the ear, which is capable of making the earth fruitful even when it sprouts mushrooms,
the royal swans, longing for Lake Mānasa and carrying bits of lotus stalks as provisions for the journey, will become your companions in the sky all the way to Kailāsa.
Take leave of this lofty mountain, your dear friend, embracing him whose slopes are marked by the footprints of the Lord of the Raghus—footprints worthy of worship by men;
for from time to time, upon meeting with you, he manifests his affection by shedding warm tears born of long separation.
First, O cloud, hear from me as I speak the path corresponding to your journey; thereafter you shall hear my message, which is a draught for the ears.
Tired again and again, you shall set foot upon the mountain peaks, and where you are exhausted, you shall drink the light waters of the flowing streams.
"Is the wind carrying away the peak of the mountain?"— thus watched with wide-eyed alarm by the innocent wives of the Siddhas looking upwards, you, your vigor observed,
should fly up from this place of lush Nicula trees toward the sky facing north, avoiding on the path of the world-elephants the insolence of their massive trunks.
This fragment of Indra’s bow, appearing before you like a blending of jewel-lustres, emerges from the top of an anthill;
with it, your dark body will attain an exceeding beauty, just as Viṣṇu in his cowherd guise did with a peacock feather of shimmering luster.

Drunk in by the eyes of the village women—eyes moist with affection and ignorant of the play of the brow that says "the fruit of agriculture depends on you"—ascend the Māla plateau, fragrant from the recent turning of the furrows; then proceed a little westward with a swift pace, and once more turn toward the north.
Mount Āmrakūṭa will properly bear you upon its peak—exhausted by the fatigue of the journey and having quenched the forest fires with its showers—as one does a guest;
for even a lowly person does not turn away from providing refuge when a friend arrives seeking it out of regard for past favors, much less one who is so exalted.

When you, who possess the hue of a smooth braid of hair, have ascended to the peak, the mountain—its slopes covered by mango trees shining with ripened fruit—will surely attain a state worthy of being gazed upon by celestial couples: dark in the center like the breast of the Earth, and pale with its remaining expanse.
Having stayed for a moment in that bower enjoyed by the wives of forest-dwellers, you— your pace now quickened by the discharge of water—
will cross the further path and behold the Revā river at the rocky foot of the Vindhya mountains, broken apart like the decorative patterns painted on the body of an elephant.
Having taken its water, which is scented with the bitter ichor of wild elephants and whose current is checked by groves of *jambū* trees, you should proceed after shedding your rain;
for the wind will not be able to shake you, O Cloud, as you possess internal substance—for the empty becomes light, while fullness leads to weight.
Seeing the *nīpa* tree greenish-brown with half-grown filaments, and the *kandalī* plants along the marshy banks with their first buds appearing;
and having smelled the fragrance of the earth, which is even more sweet in burnt forests, those deer will indicate the path for you as the clouds shed drops of water.
I foresee, my friend, that even though you desire to depart quickly for the sake of my beloved, there will be delay for you at every mountain fragrant with *kakubha* flowers;
for you will be greeted by peacocks with tearful eyes and white-cornered glances, welcoming you with their cries—how then can you resolve to go swiftly?
With grove-fences pale in hue from *ketaka* flowers pierced by their needle-like thorns, with village shrines bustling with the nest-building of domestic crows,
and with the edges of their rose-apple forests darkened by ripening fruit, the Daśārṇa country will, upon your arrival, become a place where swans remain for only a few days.
Having gone to their capital city, renowned by the name Vidiśā and situated in those directions, you shall immediately obtain even the great fruit of your amorous longing:
you shall drink the sweet water of the Vetravatī river, which is as beautiful as a face with its arching brows, made charming by the sound of its waves lapping against the banks.

There you should dwell upon the mountain named Nīcairghoṣa for the sake of rest, which seems to thrill with joy at your touch through its *kadamba* trees in full bloom; there, by means of its stone grottoes exhaling the fragrance of the dalliance of courtesans, it proclaims the unrestrained youthfulness of the city-dwellers.
Resting there, you shall sprinkle with fresh droplets of water the buds of jasmine in the gardens growing on the banks of the forest rivers;
and by providing shade, you will become momentarily acquainted with the faces of the flower-gatherers, whose ear-lotuses are withered by the pain of wiping away perspiration from their cheeks.
Although the path you have set out upon toward the northern quarter is circuitous, do not be averse to the embrace of Ujjayinī’s palatial mansions;
for if you do not take delight in the eyes of the city women there—eyes startled by flashes of lightning and with tremulous outer corners—you shall be utterly cheated.

On the way, become one who tastes the essence of the Nirvindhyā river as she glides along—she whose girdle-string is the rows of birds warbling amidst the agitation of her waves, and who reveals her navel in the form of her eddies with a charming faltering of her flow; for in the presence of lovers, the first word of affection from women is indeed a playful coquetry.

O fortunate one, as you pass by the Sindhu, whose thin waters have become like braided hair and whose banks bear a pale hue from the withered leaves falling from the trees growing upon them, she reveals her beauty through the state of separation; you must therefore provide that very means by which she may abandon her emaciation.
Having reached Avanti, where the village elders are experts in the stories of Udayana, follow the city previously mentioned, Viśālā, which is vast in its splendor;

it is like a radiant fragment of heaven brought down to earth by the remaining merits of those celestial beings who have gone to the ground when the fruits of their good deeds had nearly been exhausted.
Where, at dawn, the breeze from the Siprā— prolonging the sharp and honeyed warbling of the cranes, rendered fragrant by its friendship with the scent of blooming lotuses,
and caressing the limbs— removes the exhaustion of women’s lovemaking, like a beloved lover offering flattering entreaties.

Having spent the night in her palaces— fragrant with flowers and marked by the red lac from the feet of lovely women— he, his body refreshed by the incense for grooming the hair wafting from the lattices, and having been offered the gift of a dance by the domestic peacocks out of affection for their kin, felt his inner soul weary from the journey.
Regarded with reverence by the Gaṇas as having the hue of your master’s neck, may you go to the holy abode of Caṇḍeśvara, the teacher of the three worlds,

where the gardens are shaken by breezes from the Gandhavatī river— breezes fragrant with the pollen of blue water-lilies and pungent from the bath-water of young women intent on sporting in the stream.
O Cloud, even if you reach Mahākāla at some other time, you must remain there until the sun passes beyond the range of your vision;
by serving as a praiseworthy drum for the evening offerings to the Wielder of the Trident, you shall obtain the full fruit of your deep-thundering roars.
There, the courtesans— their girdles jingling with the sound of their footsteps, their hands weary from waving fly-whisks whose handles are encircled by the play of gemstone reflections—
having received from you the first drops of rain that bring pleasure to the marks of your fingernails, will cast upon you side-long glances as long as a swarm of bees.
Thereafter, having merged into a circle [of light] within the forest of tall boughed trees, bearing the twilight radiance red as a fresh *japā* flower,
satisfy the desire of Hara— the Lord of Creatures— for the moist elephant-hide at the commencement of his dance, while your devotion is watched by Bhavānī with eyes stilled and free from agitation.

As women travel there at night toward their lovers' dwellings along the royal road, where all light is blocked by darkness thick enough to be pierced by a needle, show them the path with a flash of lightning as smooth as a streak of gold on a touchstone; yet, do not be loud with thunder after the release of rain, for they are timid.

Having spent that night on some palace balcony where the pigeons are asleep, with your consort the lightning exhausted from long play, you may once again traverse the remainder of the journey when the sun is seen; for friends who have undertaken a task for their friend do not indeed delay.
At that time, lovers must pacify the tears of their neglected wives; therefore, quickly leave the path of the sun.
For he too has returned to wipe away the dew-tears from the lotus-face of the night-lily, and if you obstruct his rays, he will feel no small measure of resentment toward you.
When the waters of this deep river are as clear as the mind, even your reflection—naturally beautiful—will find entry within them.
Therefore, out of steadfastness, you ought not to let her glances, bright as white water-lilies and darting like the leaping of minnows, go in vain.

Having stolen her dark garment of water—which clings as if held by her hand, which has reached the branches of the reeds, and which has abandoned its banks as if they were her hips—your departure, my friend, will be accomplished with great difficulty as you hang over it; for who, having once tasted the pleasure of one whose thighs are exposed, is capable of abandoning her?
A cool breeze, delightful from its contact with the fragrance of the earth revived by the outpouring of your own essence, being drunk in by elephants through the pleasant resonance of their temples,
will blow gently as you approach the mountain that precedes the gods, bringing to ripeness the *udumbara* fruits of the forest.

There, making yourself a cloud of flowers, may you bathe Skanda—who has made his dwelling permanent—by means of showers of blossoms upon that mountain whose peaks are moistened by the waters of the celestial Gaṅgā;
for that splendor, which surpasses the sun and was gathered from the mouth of the Fire-god, exists for the sake of protecting Indra’s armies against the wearer of the new moon.

Afterwards, you should cause that peacock of Pāvaka to dance with thundering roars, heavy from seizing the mountain peaks— the peacock whose fallen plumage, encircled by streaks of light, Bhavānī places upon her ear out of love for her son, reaching as far as the petal of a blue lotus, its outer corner washed by the luster of Hara’s moon.

Having worshipped this god born in the forest of reeds (Śaravaṇabhava) and having traversed the road— your path cleared by pairs of Siddhas carrying lutes for fear of water droplets— you should descend [to the river],
honoring the fame of Rantideva which was born from the sacrifice of cows and which has transformed into a stream upon the earth.

When you, the thief of Śārṅgin’s complexion, bend down to take water from her, the sky-dwellers will gaze from afar with eyes cast downward at that river’s current— which, though broad, appears slender due to its distance— like a single string of pearls from the earth with a large sapphire in its center.

Having crossed that river, proceed, making your own form the object of the curious glances of the women of Daśapura— glances whose playful movements are familiar with the arching of creeper-like brows, whose dark and variegated luster shines above as the lashes are raised, and which steal the beauty of bees following the scattering of *kunda* flowers.
Descending with your shadow upon the land of Brahmāvarta, you should resort to that Kuru field which betokens the great battle of the kṣatriyas;
there, with hundreds of sharp arrows, the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow showered the faces of the princes as you do lotuses with your downpour of rain.

O gentle one, having abandoned the waters of the Revatī, which possess a most pleasing taste and are marked by the glances of beautiful women, and having turned away from battle out of affection for his kin, Balarāma resorted to those waters of the Sarasvatī; by approaching them, you shall become pure within, remaining black only in outward appearance.
Therefore, you should go to the daughter of Jahnu at Anukanakhala, who descended from the king of mountains as a flight of stairs to heaven for the sons of Sagara;
she who, as if laughing with her foam at the knitting of Gaurī’s eyebrows, seized the hair of Śambhu with her wave-hands clinging to the moon.
If, like a celestial elephant hanging from the rear half of its body in the sky to drink from it, you should gaze askance at its water, which is as clear as pure crystal, then she—
by your shadow suddenly gliding upon the stream— would become as beautiful as the confluence of the Yamunā reached out of place.
Having reached that very mountain, the source of that [river], whose rocks are perfumed by the musk of seated deer and which is white with snow,
you— seated upon its peak to dispel the fatigue of the journey— will possess a splendor comparable to the mud dug up by the white bull of the three-eyed Lord Śiva.

If, as the wind blows, a forest fire born from the friction of the trunks of *sarala* trees should afflict you—its flames consuming the bushy tails of yaks—then you ought to extinguish it with thousands of streams of water; for the wealth of the noble has as its fruit the alleviation of the suffering of those in distress.

But those śarabhas who, unable to endure your roar, shall out of arrogant pride attempt to leap over you—the one who should not be leaped over—in order to break their own limbs, you should scatter them with a laugh-like shower of tumultuous sparks; for who indeed does not become an object of contempt when their efforts are directed toward a fruitless undertaking?
There, bowing with devotion, you should circumambulate the clearly visible footprint of the moon-crested Lord upon the rock, to which offerings are constantly presented by the Siddhas;
for upon seeing it, those who possess faith, their sins shaken off, become fit for the attainment of his eternal station among the Gaṇas after the departure of the senses.
The hollow bamboos, being filled by the winds, resound sweetly; the Kinnarīs sing the victory over Tripura with impassioned voices.
If your own sound should ring out resonant like a drum within the caves, then indeed the entire purpose of the music of Paśupati will be realized there.

Having passed those various wonders on the slopes of the Snowy Mountain, you should follow toward the northern direction through the Krauñca-cleft— the gateway for swans and the path to the glory of Bhṛgupati— which is dark and long-stretched, resembling the left foot of Viṣṇu as he prepares to subdue Bali.
And having gone upward, you shall become a guest of Kailāsa, whose mountain ridges were heaved up by the arms of the Ten-faced one and which serves as a mirror for the women of the gods;
it stands pervading the sky with its lily-white peaks, like the massed, loud laughter of the Three-eyed Lord spreading out in every direction.
I foresee that when you, resembling smooth crushed collyrium, stand upon its slope, the playful grace of that mountain— now as white as the freshly severed tusk of an elephant—
will become a sight to be gazed upon with steady eyes, like a dark garment draped over the shoulder of the wielder of the plow.
And if Gaurī, having left behind her serpent-bracelet and being given a hand by Śambhu, should wander on foot upon that pleasure-mountain, then you—
having assumed a form composed of various graceful curves and having solidified the mass of water within— you must serve as a staircase, providing a pleasant touch for her feet during her ascents.
There, the celestial maidens will surely lead you to serve as a fountain-house, with water sprayed forth by the striking of their bracelets against their vajra-jewels.
O friend, if you do not wish to be released from them when seized by the heat, you must terrify those women, who are eager for play, with thunderclaps harsh to the ear.
Taking from Lake Mānasa water that produces golden lotuses, and at his pleasure providing for Airāvaṇa the delight of a momentary face-veil with its spray, he—
shaking the garments of the wish-fulfilling trees with breezes carrying droplets of water and distinguished by his own shade— shall enter that king of mountains, which is as clear as crystal.

O wanderer at will, having seen Alakā upon his lap—where the Ganges flows like a slipped silken garment as if in love—you shall not fail to recognize it again; there, at the proper time, her lofty palaces carry forth clouds that emit torrents of water, like a passionate woman whose locks are woven with strings of pearls.
Where palaces— possessing lovely women like clouds with lightning, adorned with paintings like those with rainbows, with the sound of drums beaten for music like the deep, resonant rumble of thunder,
with jeweled floors containing water within, and with lofty peaks scraping the sky— are fully capable of rivaling you through these various shared characteristics.
Where the young women held a play-lotus in their hands, their tresses were interwoven with young *kunda* flowers, the beauty of their faces was turned pale by the pollen of *lodhra* blossoms,
fresh *kurabaka* was in their braided hair, lovely *śirīṣa* at their ears, and *nīpa* flowers— born from your arrival— at the parting of their hair.
In that city, Yakṣas, accompanied by their most excellent wives, resort to palace terraces made of white jewels, which are adorned with the reflections of stars as if they were flowers;
there, while your deep-sounding drums are slowly beaten upon their surfaces, they enjoy honey produced by the *kalpavṛkṣa* trees, which has pleasure as its fruit.

There, the moonstones— suspended from webs of thread and dripping with clear drops of water— dispel the exhaustion born of lovemaking from the limbs of women embraced and fanned by the arms of their beloveds, as they are awakened by the moonbeams brightened by the removal of your obstruction.
Where clouds like you, led by the wind to the upper stories of the palaces, immediately cause damage to the paintings with their spray of water droplets,
then— seized by fear as it were— rush out through the lattices, shattered and skilled at mimicking columns of smoke.
There, when their lovers— hands unsteady with passion— impetuously snatch away the garments of the Yakṣa maidens, loosened by the slackening of the knot at the waist,
the handfuls of scented powder thrown by those women, bewildered by shame, become fruitless efforts even as they reach the jewel-lamps that stand high upon the pillars.

Where, at the rising of the sun, the nocturnal path of amorous women is indicated by *mandāra* flowers fallen from their tresses due to the trembling of their gait, by golden lotuses with cut leaves slipped from their ears, by nets of pearls whose threads were snapped against their breasts, and by necklaces.
Knowing that the God who is the friend of the Lord of Wealth dwells there in person, the god of love generally does not carry his bow out of fear;

yet his endeavor is accomplished solely by the graceful movements of beautiful women, which are unfailing upon their targets—the hearts of lovers—through the casting of glances accompanied by the knitting of eyebrows.
There, to the north of the house of the Lord of Wealth, is our home, visible from afar by its gateway as beautiful as a rainbow;
in its garden stands a young *mandāra* tree, nurtured by my beloved as if he were her own son, which bends low with clusters of blossoms reachable by the hand.
And in this place there is a pond with steps made of emerald stone, strewn with golden lotus buds having lustrous beryl stalks;
the swans dwelling in its waters, their sorrows dispelled, will no longer long for Lake Mānasa even upon seeing you nearby.
On its bank stands a pleasure-mound with peaks fashioned of exquisite sapphires, beautiful to behold with its surrounding hedge of golden plantain trees;
seeing you, O friend, with lightning flashing at your edges, my heart grows anxious as I remember that very spot, thinking, "It is dear to my wife."
Here, near the mādhavī bower surrounded by a hedge of kuravaka flowers, stand the lovely red aśoka with its trembling shoots and the kesara;
one longs for your friend’s left foot along with me, while the other, under the pretext of a ritual requirement, desires the wine from her mouth.
And in its center stands a golden perch with a crystal surface, fixed at its base with jewels that have the luster of not-yet-fully-grown bamboo;
upon it, at the close of day, sits your friend the peacock, made to dance by my beloved with the clapping of her hands, which are made beautiful by jingling bracelets.
O virtuous one, you should recognize [me] by these characteristics held in your heart; and having seen Śaṅkha and Padma with their forms painted near the door, you will know me.
Indeed, this palace must now have its luster dimmed by my absence; for surely a lotus does not retain its own splendor when the sun has departed.
Having immediately assumed the small body of a young elephant for the sake of a swift descent, you should sit upon the lovely peak of the pleasure-mountain previously mentioned;
there, you ought to cause the flash of lightning—falling into the interior of the house—to appear as a faint glimmer, resembling the flickering of a swarm of fireflies.
Slender, dark-complexioned, with pointed teeth and lips like the ripe *bimba* fruit, thin-waisted, with the glance of a startled doe and a deep-set navel;
moving slowly from the weight of her hips, slightly bent by her breasts—she who might exist there would be, among the realm of young women, as if the Creator’s very first creation.
You should know her to be one of few words, my second life, like a solitary female ruddy goose when I, her mate, have gone far away;
as these heavy days pass, I think that young woman, filled with intense longing, has changed her very appearance like a lotus plant withered by the frost.

Surely her face—its eyes swollen from intense weeping, its lower lip discolored by the heat of many sighs, and resting upon her hand—is partially obscured by hanging tresses; thus it bears the wretchedness of the moon, whose beauty is marred when you approach it.

She will soon fall within your sight—either busy with her offerings, or painting a likeness of me emaciated by separation as she contemplates its inner meaning, or perhaps questioning the sweet-voiced sarika bird in its cage: "O connoisseur, do you remember your husband? For you were indeed his beloved."
Or perhaps, O gentle one, having placed the lute upon her lap covered by a soiled garment, she desires to sing a song composed with verses marked by my name;
yet, having somehow managed to tune the strings which were dampened by her tears, she repeatedly forgets even the melodic modulations (mūrcchanā) she herself had fashioned.

Either counting the remaining months by means of flowers scattered on the threshold as a tally for the period fixed from the day of separation, or relishing through imagination the pleasures of union with their mental inception already set in the heart— these, generally speaking, are the diversions of women during the absence of their lovers.
During the day, separation does not afflict your virtuous friend so much when she is occupied with her duties; however, I fear that at night, being without diversion, her grief will be even heavier.
Therefore, standing at the window near her bed upon the ground at midnight, look upon her as she lies awake and comfort her with my messages.
Emaciated by longing, sitting on one side upon her bed of separation—resembling the slender crescent of the moon remaining as a mere digit at the edge of the eastern mountain;
she who spent that very night, which I passed with me in moments of desired dalliance, now enduring it in its full length of separation with hot tears.
She was tossing her long, matted hair—which hung down as far as her cheeks and had become coarse from bathing in pure water—by means of sighs that distressed her bud-like lower lip;
she longed for sleep, in which even a dream-union with me might somehow occur, yet found no opportunity for it due to the pressure of tears from her eyes.

On the first day of our separation, she bound her hair into a single braid, casting aside her wreath; at the end of the curse, when her grief has dissolved, I shall untie that very braid—now rough and uneven—which she repeatedly brushes from the curve of her cheek with her hand, its nails untrimmed and soiled by the touch.

Covering her eyes—weighed down by tears from exhaustion—with lashes that seemed to have entered the path of the moon’s net of rays, cool with nectar; eyes that had turned toward him out of former affection and then withdrawn just as before; she was like a land-lotus on a cloudy day, neither fully blossomed nor asleep.

Having cast off her ornaments, that frail woman, holding her body—which has been repeatedly pressed against the surface of the bed with agonizing pain—will surely cause even you to shed tears of fresh water; for generally, everyone whose inner soul is moistened becomes moved by compassion.
I know that your friend’s heart is filled with affection for me; therefore, I infer her state of mind during this first separation.
It is not that a sense of self-importance makes me so talkative, O fortunate one; rather, my brother, everything I have said will soon be evident to you directly.
With the movement of its outer corners blocked by her tresses, devoid of the gloss of collyrium, and having forgotten its play of the eyebrows due to her abstention from wine—
when you draw near, I suspect that the doe-eyed girl’s eye, throbbing at the upper lid, will attain the beauty of a trembling blue lotus from the agitation of its fish-like pupil.
And her left thigh— now being freed from the nail-marks of my fingers, having by the turn of fate been made to cast off its long-accustomed net of pearls,
and accustomed to being massaged by my hand at the end of our lovemaking— that thigh, fair as the trunk of a fresh plantain tree, shall tremble.
O Cloud, at that time, if she should have found the comfort of sleep, sit beside her and endure for just one watch, refraining from thundering;
let there not be a firm embrace with her arms entwined around my neck—lost as I am in a dream of my beloved—suddenly broken by your roar.

Having raised her up and comforted her with a breeze cooled by your own spray, you should approach that proud woman— who has her eyes fixed upon the window occupied by you and who is like a *mālatī* flower newly covered in buds— while she stands within the lightning-filled interior, and address her with words as steady as your thunder.
"O lady whose husband lives, know me to be the beloved friend of your lord, a cloud come into your presence with his messages held in my heart;
I am he who, with deep and tender sounds, urges on the crowds of weary travelers on the road who long for their wives to loosen their braided hair."

When this has been told, O gentle one, she—looking up at you with a heart swelling with longing like Maithilī at the sight of the son of the Wind, and honoring you with her gaze—will listen with rapt attention to what follows; for to women, news of a beloved brought by a friend is but little short of an actual reunion.

"O long-lived one, for my sake and to do yourself a favor, you should speak thus to her: 'Your companion, staying at the hermitage of Rāmagiri, is unharmed; O frail lady, being separated from you, he asks after your welfare—this alone is the primary concern for living beings who easily encounter misfortune.'"

With limb against limb— his own slender body against her slender one, his feverishly burning frame against hers who is drenched in tears, his heart of incessant longing against hers who yearns for him,
and his hot sighs against hers who sighs even more heavily— he, whose path is blocked by hostile fate, enters her through those very mental constructs while standing far away.

That which you were eager to whisper into the ear of your friends before them out of a longing to touch their faces—even that which was expressible by words has now passed beyond the range of hearing and been unseen by your eyes; yet, with its words composed out of longing, it says this to you through my mouth.
I perceive your limbs in the *śyāmā* creepers, your glances in the eyes of startled does, the radiance of your face in the moon, and your tresses in the plumage of peacocks;
I see the play of your eyebrows in the slender ripples of rivers. Alas, O fierce one, your likeness is not found anywhere in a single place!
Having painted you upon a stone with mineral pigments while feigning anger out of love, I wish to depict myself fallen at your feet;
yet before I can do so, my vision is repeatedly obscured by welling tears—for cruel Fate does not permit our union even in that [representation].
As you were somehow found by me in my dream-visions for the sake of a merciless embrace with my arms outstretched toward the sky,
surely many tears as thick as pearls did not fall from the local deities who watched me upon the sprouts of the trees?

O virtuous lady, those breezes from the snowy mountain, which immediately burst open the leaf-buds of the deodar trees and proceed toward the south fragrant with the flow of their resin—should they have previously touched your limbs, O worthy one, I would embrace them. (KMgD 104)
How might this night of three watches, with its long hours, be shortened like a mere moment? And how might even the day have its heat become faint in all its states?
O lady with tremulous eyes, my heart—its desires difficult to attain—is thus rendered helpless by the intense fevers of the pain of separation from you.
"Indeed, though I reflect much upon myself, I find no support within my own soul; therefore, O auspicious lady, you too must by no means succumb to despondency.
For whom has absolute happiness ever arrived, or suffering in its entirety? Circumstances move downward and upward like the rim of a wheel."
"My curse shall end when the wielder of the Śārṅga bow rises from his serpent-bed; close your eyes for four other months.
Afterwards, we two shall enjoy each of those desires of our own hearts, multiplied by our separation, during nights lit by the full autumnal moonlight."

Furthermore, she said: "Formerly, while we were lying in bed, you fell asleep with your neck entwined in mine; then, having woken up and begun to weep somewhat loudly, I spoke repeatedly with a suppressed laugh to you who was questioning me.
And you said to me: 'O rogue, I saw you in a dream delighting some other woman.'"
Knowing from this gift of proof that I am well, O dark-eyed one, do not become distrustful of me because of public rumor.
They say that affections diminish somewhat during separation; for when one does not enjoy a beloved object, those feelings grow intense and become a mass of love.
O gentle one, have you indeed resolved upon this service to your kin for me? From your silence, I certainly do not judge your steadfastness;
for even without a sound, you grant water when requested by the cātakas, for the very act of fulfilling the desired object is the response of the virtuous toward those who seek their favor.

Having done this favor for me—who has followed the path of an improper request—whether out of friendship or out of a sense of compassion for me as one who is distressed, wander through your desired regions, O cloud, with your beauty enhanced by the rainy season; and may you never, even for a moment, suffer separation from the lightning.
Thus ends the *Meghadūta* composed by Kālidāsa.
